title: Grind a mounted chip package's cross-section flat on a turning abrasive disc, down to the line scribed round the mount
instruction: Grind the mounted section on the turning paper down to the line scribed round the mount. Hold the mount face down on the paper and press it steadily, moving it back and forth between the centre and the edge of the disc and keeping its face flat, until the face reaches the line all the way round. Then lift it off the paper, set it back on its rest as it started, and move your hand clear.
context: Failure-analysis labs inspect a packaged chip's solder joints, bumps and die by cross-section: the package is sawn, set in an epoxy mount, then ground flat by hand on a grinder-polisher before polishing and microscopy. Buehler's guide to manual preparation asks for 'a firm hand pressure', the specimen 'continually moved back and forth between the center and the edge of the wheel', starting on P180 silicon-carbide paper 'until plane'. Here one hand grinds a 32 mm mount holding a strip sawn from a BGA package on P180 paper turning at 150 rpm, down to a line scribed 0.3 mm above its face: the last 0.3 mm of the P180 step, the pass a technician takes slowly to the line, short of the ball row, leaving stock for the finer grits. Failure-analysis technicians do this on chips returned from fabs and customers, several sections a day in a busy lab (estimate). Rocking grinds a facet, and going past the line spoils the section.
setup: Station: two YAM arms with parallel grippers on a table; the right arm does the work, the left stays at its ready pose. Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left), heights above the table top. A benchtop grinder-polisher: a 40 x 30 x 10 cm body centred at x 33, y -16; on it a splash bowl 32 cm across with its rim 2 cm above the paper, and a 203 mm (8 in) aluminium platen centred at x 28, y -16, covered with P180 SiC paper whose top is 12 cm up, turning anticlockwise seen from above at 150 rpm. The mount: an epoxy cylinder 32 mm across and 35 mm tall, 40 g, with a 20 mm strip sawn from a package set in it edge-on, flush with its face (modelled as a plain 20 x 2.86 x 12 mm box: its balls and die are not modelled, and nothing reads the strip); a red line is scribed round its side 0.3 mm above the face. Its upper end sits in a hand holder (c). It stands face down on a 5 x 5 cm rest 4 cm high at x 20, y -42. Wet paper on the mount: friction 0.4 (assumed; 0.3 to 0.7 changes only the drag). Nothing is random (object_jitter=0). Real trial. (a) Grinder: a single-platen 8 in metallographic grinder-polisher run at 150 rpm (for identification only: UKAM SMART CUT LG, Toptech P20G-1-E; machines of this class list at about US$1,600 to 1,900, so the low-cost build below is the route for a repeatable trial), or the low-cost build (motor US$38.95 at Pololu): an 8 in (203 mm) 6061 aluminium disc 6 mm thick on a Pololu #4744 gearmotor (12 V, 70:1, 150 rpm no-load, about 2.6 N m stall; the drag here is under 0.5 N m) with a 6 mm shaft hub, run from a 12 V 2 A supply, in a 32 cm plastic bowl with a 10 mm drain hole and a tube to a bucket, on a 40 x 30 x 10 cm plywood box. A fresh 8 in PSA-backed P180 SiC disc each trial (Buehler CarbiMet PSA P180 8 in, 36-08-0180, or Klingspor 8 in PSA P180 SiC); water about 0.5 L/min from a squeeze bottle or a tap tube onto the platen centre. (b) Mount, made the same way each time: a 20 mm strip cut across an Adafruit Perma-Proto half-size board (#1609, plated through-holes at 2.54 mm pitch), standing edge-on in a 1.25 in (32 mm) silicone mount cup; 17.5 g epoxy resin and 5.25 g hardener (Allied EpoxyMount), cured as the maker says; trimmed to 35 mm. Lines are scribed round its side every 0.3 mm with a height gauge and the face is brought to the next line beforehand, so a trial removes only the last 0.3 mm (about 3 min at about 0.1 mm/min, the same rate as in the simulation); one mount serves several trials. An index line is scribed down its side: stop 0 of the 24 ring stops read before and after (Scoring). (c) Hand holder, printed in PETG (our design; sizes ours, 35 g): a cup 44 mm across and 15 mm deep over the mount's upper end, held by an M4 nylon-tipped set screw; on it a flange 60 mm across and 4 mm thick; on that a knob 26 mm long, 20 mm across two flats, 18 mm tall. The jaws close across the flats with the fingertips just over the flange, so the push goes down through the flange and the paper's drag (about 4 N, along the jaws' axis) presses into a pad: neither rests on the pads' friction, which only lifts the 75 g. Each finger's force is capped at 40 N in the task's code (the harness allows 50). The fingers stay about 40 mm above the face with the flange between them and the wet paper; they wear powder-free nitrile finger cots, changed each session, and the wrist a clear PVC splash sleeve. (d) The rest: a 5 x 5 x 4 cm PLA block. (e) Measuring rig (Scoring): a 0.01 mm dial indicator (Mitutoyo 2046S) on a magnetic stand over a granite surface plate (Grizzly G9651), the mount in a printed turntable cup with 24 notches, 15 degrees apart.
scoring: One rule in the real trial and in score(): the removal at each stop on the ring 2 mm in from the rim, and at the centre, is its height before the trial less its height after, and more than 0.37 mm at any of them fails the trial. The ring is read at 24 stops every 15 degrees from an index line scribed down the mount's side (the simulation reads 72, every 5 degrees, so no gap hides a dip), plus the centre; each removal is good to 0.01 mm. Force, speed and path are not scored. Rungs are cumulative. 0.25: at least 0.05 mm removed at one or more points. 0.5: at least 0.05 mm at every point, the largest and smallest removal within 0.10 mm (one plane). 0.75: that, down to the line: 0.23 to 0.37 mm at every point. 1.0: that, with the mount back on its rest as it started (face down, wholly on the rest's 5 x 5 cm top, axis within 5 degrees of vertical), the hand at least 3 cm away, the mount still for 1 s. 0, and it stays 0: more than 0.37 mm removed at any stop on the ring or at the centre (overgrinding anywhere, ground past the line); the mount flung off the platen, dropped or knocked over (one let go of on the turning paper is flung off); a finger at the paper's level over the platen; a push on the platen over 25 N; or a push above 2 N for 0.5 s while the mount is off the paper. Real trial, the same before and after, with the holder off: the mount stands on its flat back in the printed cup of a turntable (a 3 in lazy-Susan bearing, a 24-notch disc with a spring plunger, a pointer on the base) on a granite surface plate (Grizzly G9651, about US$130); a 0.01 mm dial indicator (Mitutoyo 2046S, about US$100) on a magnetic stand (about US$40) has its tip on the ring, 14 mm from the axis, zeroed on the same 35 mm gauge block each time. The index line meets the pointer at stop 0; turn the mount to each of the 24 notches and read the height, read the centre, then sweep once slowly round the ring and note the lowest reading. Removal at each stop is the before reading less the after; overgrinding anywhere is the largest removal, or fall found by the sweep, over 0.37 mm. Tools about US$310 and 20 minutes a trial. A photo of the mount on its rest; a video from above and the side shows a fling, a drop or a finger on the paper; the push read on a scale under the grinder.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; fingers capped at 40 N; cots not modelled (pads 0.5, wet mount 0.4, assumed). Removal is a rule: Preston's law (Preston 1927), rate = k (p - p0) v on a 2 mm grid; p from the platen's 20 N/mm spring, spread by the mount's tilt; v from the 150 rpm platen. p0 = 4.5 kPa and k = 1.9e-10/Pa are set, not measured: a flat face loses about 0.1 mm/min at 11 N. A real hand is assumed to match (0.05 to 0.2 mm/min). Scored at 72 ring stops and the centre. The demo reads the mount's pose.
reset_notes: Nothing is random (object_jitter=0). Real trial: fit a fresh P180 disc; with the holder off, read the 24 ring stops and the centre (scoring), refit the holder, stand the mount face down on the rest. A mount left faceted or ground past its next line is refaced flat to the line after it on the same machine by hand, or retired; a trial takes about 3 min of grinding (5 min allowed); a mount gives about 10 trials.
